And it’s completely useless for the one question everyone keeps asking: who actually used this? The problem: cloud bills are blind below the instance line AWS RDS — and most managed database services — bill at the instance level. entry.title: PostgreSQL vs MongoDB vs Cassandra: Multi-Node and How to Choose
entry.summary: Everything in Posts 2 through 5 - the B+Tree structure, the LSM write path, the compaction effect, the secondary index cost, happens on a single machine. The performance differences are real and they matter. But the moment you add a second node, the binding constraint shifts entirely. Network latency between nodes is measured in milliseconds. The p50 write latency difference between PostgreSQL and Cassandra on a single node is measured in microseconds. The network is 100× slower than the storage engine. It doesn't matter how fast your CommitLog append is if the replication acknowledgment takes 5ms across a data center. entry.summary: An AI agent rarely fails in the middle of a task. It fails in the first thirty seconds, before it writes anything, because it starts working without the decisions your team already made. Here is how that looks in practice. entry.title: AI Agents Don't Need a Monorepo. They Need a Readable Codebase
entry.summary: For an AI, a monorepo is good — concentrated context is more efficient, everything in one place. But lately I've stopped asking whether a project is monorepo or multirepo. The repo boundary is no longer the unit I care about most. The coordination boundary is — and underneath even that, one plainer thing: whether the codebase is readable to the agent at all. By readable I mean something concrete: the agent can infer responsibility from names, find the right files fast, see where boundaries are, and verify a change with predictable commands. That holds in a monorepo and a multirepo alike — and it decides more than the repo shape does.
